newsitem.title: FRANCE: Trial of Algerian FIS leader opens in Algeria.
newsitem.headline: Trial of Algerian FIS leader opens in Algeria.

text.p: Islamist leader Abdelkader Hachani went on trial in a tightly-guarded court in Algiers on Monday on charges of trying to undermine state security, after more than five years of detention without trial.

Hachani, a former oil engineer, led the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) to a landslide first-round victory in Algeria's first multi-party general election in 1991. The authorities cancelled the ballot in January 1992, sparking violence in which about 60,000 people have died.
Eyewitnesses told Reuters by telephone that armed troops and paramilitary gendarmes ringed the court building in central Algiers from early Monday morning.
The court is on Abane Ramdane street, running parallel to the seafront. Traffic was being diverted and the road blocked.
Hachani, now aged around 40, is represented by a team of lawyers, headed by Ali Yahia Abdennour and Mustapha Bouchachi.
In a statement apparently signed by him back in January 1992, Hachani had called on the army not to be the "strike force" of the "junta of power".
The court's first session on Monday was devoted to procedural argument on calling witnesses, including high-profile personalities and officials, an eyewitness said.
Hachani, shortly after the 1992 cancellation of the election, forecast his arrest, saying: "I know that in the next few days I could be jailed and I am prepared for that."
He has since been held in Sirkadji high security prison near the Casbah, the ancient heart of old Algiers. Shortly after his arrest, the FIS was outlawed.

Viewed as a relative moderate who had called on FIS activists to avoid violence, he termed the cancellation of the poll "a coup d'etat against the Islamic state" which the FIS planned for the North African country and its 29 million people.
His party had won 188 of the 232 seats decided outright in the first round.
Hachani is being tried along with three journalists as a result of a statement which appeared in the Arabic-language Al Khabar newspaper shortly after the ballot was scrapped.
The statement apparently signed by Hachani urged members of the military to disobey orders from their officers to act against Islamist activists.
The official Algerian news agency APS said the accused faced charges of "inciting, by all methods of information, crimes and offences against state security and national unity."

Hachani was arrested on January 22, 1992 after the Defence Ministry accused him of "launching an appeal for rebellion in the army". Six police cars swooped on him in the southern Algiers suburb of Badjarah and took him off to gendarmerie headquarters.
He and the journalists are also accused of publishing "erroneous and tententious information likely to harm national interest and national unity."
The charges can bring imprisonment of up to 10 years.

Hachani took over the FIS leadership temporarily after party president Abassi Madani and his deputy Ali Belhadj were arrested, six months before the election. They were tried on charges of subversion and each sentenced in July 1992 to 12 years' jail.

Algerian newspapers last month said Hachani had been on hunger strike to try to force the authorities to put him on trial. He appeared briefly before Algiers special court in January 1995 but his trial was put off, APS said.
Special courts, set up to streamline the trials of Islamist activists and heavily criticised by human rights groups, were abolished later in 1995 after passing scores of death sentences.

Last week, the FIS executive in exile said in a statement that Hachani should be released: "This would certainly contribute to an easing of tensions required to promote the necessary climate for a return to peace and stability."

Algeria last month held the first multi-party general election since the 1992 poll cancellation. Radical Islamists were barred but two moderate Islamist parties were allowed to take part. They won a total of 103 seats in the 380-seat National Assembly.
